title: If the image-ban is a separate positive precept, Rome’s Decalogue becomes an eleven-word Hendralogus
source_text: XV. Sed si prohibitio ista, Non facies tibi sculptile, &c. sit lex quaedam positiva, ad tempus solum vetans ne ulla Dei ipsius, vel creaturae cujusvis Imago ad cultum proponatur, profecto lex illa praeceptum singulare constituit, quod non debet confundi cum primo, Non habebis Deos alienos coram me, quod praeceptum morale est, & juris mere naturalis. Ac plane aliud est, unicum Deum agnoscere, nec ullum alium pro Deo habere, & Deum illum in nulla imagine colere, nec figuram aliquam ad adorationem & cultum fabricare; praesertim ex Scholae Romanae hypothesi, quae putat eos qui Dei & Sanctorum imaginibus adorationem & cultum deferunt, nihil facere contra legem illam, non habebis Deos alienos coram me. Ac proinde in Decalogo non decem, sed undecim praecepta numerari debent: nec Decalogus sed potius Hendralogus nominari debet: cum tamen istud divinae Legis breviarium Moses nominet decem verba, id est, decem praecepta. Siquidem, prout vult Ecclesia Romana, lex de non concupiscendo duo praecepta continet, unum quo prohibetur concupiscentia Uxoris, alterum quo prohibetur concupiscentia domus alienae. Unde sequitur in secunda tabula septem esse praecepta, quibus adjungenda erunt non amplius tria, sed quatuor praecepta primae tabulae, quandoquidem prohibitio de nullis imaginibus ad cultum faciendis, necessario singulare quoddam praeceptum constituet.
pass_a_gloss: But if that prohibition, Thou shalt not make for thyself a graven thing, &c., is a certain positive law, forbidding only for a time that any Image of God himself, or of any creature whatsoever, be proposed for cult, then indeed that law constitutes a singular commandment, which ought not to be confused with the first, Thou shalt not have alien Gods before me, which is a moral commandment, and of merely natural right. And it is plainly one thing to acknowledge the one God, and to hold no other for God, and another to cultivate that God in no image, and not to fabricate any figure for adoration and cult; especially on the hypothesis of the Roman School, which thinks that those who pay adoration and cult to the images of God and of the Saints do nothing against that law, thou shalt not have alien Gods before me. And accordingly in the Decalogue not ten, but eleven commandments ought to be numbered: nor ought it to be named Decalogus but rather Hendralogus: although Moses names that breviary of the divine Law ten words, that is, ten commandments. Seeing that, as the Roman Church wills, the law concerning not coveting contains two commandments, one by which the coveting of the Wife is prohibited, another by which the coveting of another’s house is prohibited. Whence it follows that in the second table there are seven commandments, to which are to be joined not any longer three, but four commandments of the first table, seeing that the prohibition of making no images for cult necessarily constitutes a certain singular commandment.
pass_b_english: Separate the image-ban from Non habebis Deos alienos and you mint an eleventh precept.
Moses still calls the Law’s breviary ten words—so Rome’s split (plus her two covetings) drives a Hendralogus, not a Decalogue.

choices.why: Marks the first commandment as moral, not ceremonial.
